newsitem.title: USA: Martin Luther King's son meets with James Earl Ray.
newsitem.headline: Martin Luther King's son meets with James Earl Ray.

text.p: A frail James Earl Ray assured the son of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. that he did not murder his father, as television cameras captured their first-ever jailhouse meeting on Thursday.
"I just want to ask you for the record, did you kill my father?" Dexter Scott King asked.

"No, no, no, I didn't, no," Ray responded, to which King replied: "I want you to know that I believe you and my family believes you and we are going to do everything in our power to try and make sure that justice will prevail."

The two men met and shook hands for the first time in a conference room at the Lois DeBerry Special Needs Facility, where the ailing Ray, 68, has been held off and on since suffering chronic organ failure late last year.
Ray entered the room in a wheelchair but insisted on moving to a chair opposite King.
"I know this is a difficult period for you. We want to bring what has occurred in the dark into the light," King told Ray.

After the initial conversation in front of Cable News Network cameras, the two met in private where King hoped to question Ray about what, if anything, he could contribute to the numerous unanswered questions about the 1968 slaying.

King testified last month on Ray's behalf at a Memphis court hearing in which Ray's lawyers took the first step in securing a trial for Ray, who originally confessed to killing King but quickly recanted and said he was only trying to avoid the death penalty.

A Tennessee criminal appeals court panel was considering whether to grant a request to retest the rifle and the remnants of the fatal bullet with a sophisticated electron microscope. Repeated testings of the rifle markings never conclusively proved it fired the fatal bullet.

Dexter King and his mother, Coretta Scott King, asked the judge to consider that a trial could resolve the wealth of conflicting information that has emerged since the assassination. A 1978 congressional investigation concluded Ray, a petty criminal with a history of incompetence, acted alone.

But questions about how Ray managed to elude law enforcement for two months and travel to Europe after the shooting, subsequent disclosures about FBI covert probes of King's activities, and the sealed documents from the original investigations have fuelled conspiracy theories for decades.
Doctors have said Ray, who is serving a 99-year sentence, will die before the end of the year without a liver transplant.
